name: Grace Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to any company, union, party or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I operate a roof bolter underground at the Hollins Creek gold mine. After they blast and clear a new section of tunnel, I drive the bolter in and put long steel bolts up into the roof and walls so the rock doesn't come down on anyone. It's slow, careful work, and I'm slow and careful, so it suits me. I've been doing it a bit over two years. Before that my husband Erik and I ran the farm supply store in Ashby for twenty-six years, until we sold it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Why go underground at fifty-six, after selling a business?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Everybody asks that. Honestly, I was bored stupid after the sale, and my cousin's husband said the mine was short of people and paid well. I thought I'd try it for a year. What I like is that it matters, every bolt I put in is someone getting home. What I don't like is the cold at the start of a shift and feeling like the slowest person on the crew, which I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that wouldn't shock me. In the store we had three different computer systems that were going to change everything, and in the end we still counted the feed bags by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, but there's some good in it. Our shift reports are quicker now with the voice notes, so that's something. I'm not one to post about things, but I'd say that at the table at Sunday lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means I keep doing this as long as I like it, probably until sixty-two. We don't need the money, not really, the store sale set us up. I'd just keep at it and get better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. I'd do the next bolting certificate in the autumn, and I'd keep putting my pay into the savings and the grandkids' education fund. Maybe I'd go part-time a year or two earlier than planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's like hearing the weather will be the same as yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use voice notes for shift reports. Is that an AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose it is. You talk into the tablet and it writes the report. I didn't trust it at first, but after everyone else used it for a few months and it worked, I started too. I still read it over twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone at the mine be upset with this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our shift boss, Lachie, he's young and he'd love the robots. He talks about automated bolters all the time. Me, I'd be pleased. Old Joe on my crew would be over the moon.

S0.say: It was oversold but has some good in it, like faster shift reports with voice notes. She'd say it at Sunday lunch rather than online.
S0.think: She'd keep bolting as long as she enjoys it, probably to sixty-two. The sale of the store set them up, so she doesn't really need the money.
S0.do: Keeps going as she is and takes the next bolting certificate in autumn. Keeps saving her pay and adding to the grandchildren's education fund, and might go part-time a little early.
S0.feel: Calm, like a forecast that matches yesterday.
S0.quote: In the store we had three different computer systems that were going to change everything, and in the end we still counted the feed bags by hand.
S0.fieldNote: Grace works for purpose and interest more than money, which shapes everything she says. She adopts technology only after others have shown it works, as with the voice notes. Her tone is practical and unhurried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I can picture that. They've already got a bolter at another mine that does half the job by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense, as long as the company is fair to people about it. Safety bolting is a good place for machines, nobody should be under a bad roof if they don't have to be. I'd say that at work too, even if some of the old hands didn't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't worry me much. If the bolter goes semi-automatic, I'd learn it once it's settled in. And if they don't need me, I'm fifty-eight with savings, I'd go home and do the garden and see the grandkids more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the new bolters had been running for six months or so, then ask to be trained on them. I'd talk to Erik about going part-time if the hours got cut. I wouldn't change our money plans, we've already got a good few years of savings and the store money invested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit sad for the old way of doing it, but not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait six months. What are you waiting for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the problems to come out. In the store, we bought a new stock system once the day it came out and it crashed during the busiest week of spring planting. I learned my lesson. Let someone else find the bugs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe, definitely. He's been bolting for thirty years, he's sixty-one and he's got no savings to speak of, he helped his kids buy houses. If the bolter gets automated, he's got nothing else. I'd want the company to keep him on, even if it's training the young ones.

S1.say: It makes sense if the company is fair, and roof bolting is a good place for machines because nobody should be under a bad roof if they don't have to be.
S1.think: It doesn't worry her much: she'd learn the new bolter once it settles in, or go home to her garden and grandchildren if she isn't needed.
S1.do: Waits about six months after new bolters arrive, then asks for training. Talks with Erik about going part-time if hours are cut and leaves their money plans unchanged.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a bit sad for the old way of doing things.
S1.quote: Safety bolting is a good place for machines, nobody should be under a bad roof if they don't have to be.
S1.fieldNote: She's comfortable with automation in the dangerous parts of the job and would follow others into it after a waiting period. Her lesson from a failed stock system shapes that habit. Her worry goes to a colleague with no savings, not to herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very quick. I'm not sure I believe that one, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies and the government had better be sensible and not throw people out on the street. There should be a decent payout for workers and help for towns. I'd say it at work and maybe write to the local paper, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be okay. My job would go, but I'd have retired in a few years anyway. What worries me is the money we invested from the store, it's in shares, and I don't know what happens to shares when everything changes at once. Nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to our financial adviser in the first month and move some of the store money into something safer, maybe term deposits, so we're not gambling it all. I'd keep working until they let me go and take any payout. Then I'd retire early and help my daughter with the grandkids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicky, just a bit off balance, like stepping off a boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the short warning change for you, compared with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I don't get to choose my last day or how it ends. I'd rather leave because I'm ready than because a robot showed up. And with two years nobody knows what the money will do. With more time, at least the markets settle down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be okay. Is there anything that would make you not okay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the shares collapsed and stayed down, that would hurt. We'd still have the house and some savings, so we wouldn't go hungry, but the plans for travelling and helping the grandkids with university would shrink. I don't like to think about it too much.

S2.say: Companies and government should be sensible, with decent payouts for workers and help for towns. She'd say it at work and might write to the local paper for the first time.
S2.think: Her job would go, but she'd have retired soon anyway. Her worry is the store money invested in shares, because nobody knows what happens to shares when everything changes at once.
S2.do: Sees their financial adviser in the first month to move some of the store money into safer term deposits. Works until let go, takes any payout, then retires early and helps with the grandchildren.
S2.feel: Uneasy and off balance, like stepping off a boat, but not panicky.
S2.quote: I'd rather leave because I'm ready than because a robot showed up.
S2.fieldNote: For Grace the job is the smaller worry; her investments are the larger one. She is honest that she doesn't know how markets would react. Her steady style shows in her plan: careful, advised, no sudden moves beyond protecting the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like it. I'd be sixty-three, which is past when I meant to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the companies to plan properly. Train people who want to move on, give older people a good way out. That's just common sense, and I'd say it to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's almost nothing. I'd retire around sixty-two like I planned. If anything, I'd retire knowing the robots are coming in after me, which is a bit strange, but it's not my problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep bolting until sixty-two, as planned. I'd move some of the store money into safer places over a couple of years, not in a rush. I might try the AI chat tools more, because my granddaughter says they're good for planning trips and Erik and I want to see the fjords where his family came from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little curious, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the 2-year picture you'd move the money in the first month. Here it's over a couple of years. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with five years you can see it coming and the markets aren't in a panic. I'd do it slowly, a bit at a time. Erik always says don't make big decisions in a hurry, and five years means I don't have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say anything to the younger people on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lachie and the young ones to learn how to fix the robots, not just drive them. Somebody has to keep them going. That's what I'd do if I were thirty.

S3.say: Five years is enough for companies to plan properly, train people who want to move on and give older workers a good way out. That's common sense.
S3.think: It barely affects her because she'd retire around sixty-two as planned. It's a bit strange to retire knowing robots will come in after her, but it's not her problem.
S3.do: Keeps bolting until sixty-two and moves some store money into safer places slowly over two years. Uses AI chat tools more to plan a trip with Erik to see where his family came from.
S3.quote: Erik always says don't make big decisions in a hurry, and five years means I don't have to.
S3.fieldNote: The longer warning lets Grace protect her investments slowly rather than in a hurry, which is how she prefers to act. Her own job ends on schedule. She's curious about AI tools in her personal life once the pressure is off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'll be retired long before then, sitting in the garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a sensible amount of time for everyone to get ready. Young people should think hard about what they train for. Governments should plan ahead instead of waiting for trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Personally, it means nothing much for me. I'll be retired and, hopefully, travelling. My concern is the grandkids and whether there'll be work for them, or whether they'll even need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working until sixty-two and retire, as planned. I'd keep putting into the grandkids' education fund, but I'd talk with my daughter about what kind of education makes sense now. And I'd keep the store money spread out, not all in shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A small question mark about the grandkids, but no real worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years of warning change what you'd tell your grandkids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With ten years they've got time to choose well. The oldest, Freya, is fifteen, she likes animals. Maybe something with animals and people, a vet or something, I honestly don't know if robots would do that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Across all three AGI pictures, your job ends either way. Does the timing matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only a bit. It matters for the money, how the shares behave, and whether I leave when I choose. But I'm lucky, I'm near the end. If I was forty, the timing would be everything.

S4.say: Ten years is a sensible amount of time to get ready, with young people choosing training carefully and governments planning ahead instead of waiting for trouble.
S4.think: It means little for her personally because she'll be retired and hopefully travelling. Her concern is whether there'll be work for her grandchildren.
S4.do: Works until sixty-two and retires as planned. Keeps paying into the grandchildren's education fund while rethinking with her daughter what education makes sense, and keeps the store money spread out.
S4.feel: Calm, with a small question mark about her grandchildren.
S4.quote: But I'm lucky, I'm near the end. If I was forty, the timing would be everything.
S4.fieldNote: Grace recognises that her life stage protects her and says so plainly. Across the AGI pictures, timing matters to her mainly through her investments and her sense of control. Her thoughts go to her grandchildren's choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, mostly because of the money and the rush. Everyone would be making decisions in a panic. What would help is good, honest advice about where to keep savings safe, and a decent payout for workers like Joe who don't have anything put aside.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people would do with their time. I went back to work because I was bored. If robots do everything, a lot of people will be bored, not just poor. Someone should think about that.

headlineQuote: It matters, every bolt I put in is someone getting home.
portrait: Grace Hansen is a 58-year-old roof bolter operator at an underground gold mine who started two years ago, after she and her husband sold the farm supply store they ran for twenty-six years. She works for purpose and to stave off boredom more than for money, and she takes up new technology only once others have proven it. Her job is a small worry; her bigger concern in the fast AGI picture is how the store money invested in shares would hold up, which leaves her uneasy. In every other picture she is calm, retiring on schedule and turning her thoughts to her grandchildren and to a colleague with no savings.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because of the rush, the panic and what it would do to their invested savings.
whatWouldHelp: Good, honest advice about where to keep savings safe, and a decent payout for workers who have nothing put aside.
